title: Spire and Choir
premise: Astrid Sterling, a mercenary bound by an oath to a god who fell silent a generation ago, has survived by hiding in the Valley of Hush, where magic cannot follow and the godless can forget. When a child named Wren arrives speaking the First Tongue—the language in which oaths are literally binding—Astrid learns their own forgotten vow was the seal that silenced the god, and that Wren is the vessel chosen to wake it. Hunted by the Choir, remnants of the god's old faithful who want to use Wren as a weapon, Astrid must choose between breaking their oath (and dying with it) or letting the war begin again. In the end, Astrid teaches Wren to speak the First Tongue imperfectly—humanly—and the god wakes changed: not a tyrant restored, but a quiet presence that asks rather than commands, at the cost of Astrid's memories of everyone they ever loved.
about_author: Astrid Blackwood is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing dead languages before turning to fiction. They write fantasy about people whose pasts refuse to stay buried, from a farmhouse office overlooking a valley much quieter than any in their books.

chapters.title: The Valley That Forgets
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. A routine patrol along the valley's mistline establishes the rules of Astrid's hidden life: no names spoken aloud, no oaths renewed, no leaving. The emotional beat is weary contentment built on deliberate amnesia—a survival that costs something every day.

chapters.title: A Knock in Dead Winter
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. A half-frozen child appears at the door during a snowstorm, speaking words Astrid almost understands but has never been taught. The beat is dread wrapped in reluctant tenderness; Astrid takes the child in against every instinct for self-preservation.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The child's fragmented memory reveals they walked out of the mountains alone, guided by a voice only they can hear. The beat is eerie innocence—Wren trusts completely, and their trust is more frightening than any threat.

chapters.title: What the Oath Remembers
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Hearing Wren speak triggers a buried memory: the night Astrid swore the silence-oath on behalf of a dying company. The beat is vertigo—Astrid realizes their amnesia was engineered into the vow itself.

chapters.title: The Choir Sings in Ashford
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Travelers pass through the valley carrying hymnals of a new faith; Wren recognizes the notation as corrupted First Tongue. The beat is creeping recognition that hunters are closing in, seen through a child's uncomprehending eyes.

chapters.title: Thirteen Turns
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. An old comrade, Maren, arrives wounded with news: the Choir knows the vessel lives, and the moon completes its thirteenth turn at spring equinox. The beat is cornered urgency—the valley's invisibility is already failing.

chapters.title: Lessons in a Dying Language
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid begins teaching Wren the First Tongue from fragments, discovering each word spoken correctly makes Astrid remember more—and bleed more. The beat is bittersweet intimacy; teaching becomes self-destruction.

chapters.title: The God Who Went Quiet
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren recounts the last war: how the god Vael demanded total obedience, and how a mercenary company ended it at terrible cost. The beat is grief-soaked exposition that reframes Astrid's 'betrayal' as sacrifice.

chapters.title: Mistline
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The first Choir scouts cross the valley border and dissolve, but their deaths tear a hole in the mist. The beat is cold resolve—the sanctuary is now a siege position, and Astrid must decide whether to run or stand.

chapters.title: Wren's Choice
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The voice inside Wren offers to protect the valley if Wren speaks the waking-words. Wren refuses, choosing Astrid over the god. The beat is heartbreaking loyalty—the child understands the price better than the adults do.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid attempts to renew the silence-oath using Wren as anchor, but the ritual requires remembering everything being sealed away. The beat is agonizing confrontation with the self Astrid chose to bury.

chapters.title: Ashes of the Company
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Full memory returns: Astrid didn't just witness the sealing—they volunteered to carry it, trading their whole remembered life. The beat is devastating clarity about what 'survival' has actually meant.

chapters.title: The Choir Descends
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The Choir breaches the mistline in force, led by Cantor Ilse, who believes waking Vael will restore paradise. The beat is overwhelming assault—the valley burns, and hiding ends forever.

chapters.title: Hymnal and Blade
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid fights through the Choir to reach Wren, killing former comrades-turned-fanatics. The beat is furious grief—every death is a name Astrid just recovered, paid for in blood.

chapters.title: Cantor Ilse
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Her conviction is revealed as genuine: she watched her family starve in the godless years and believes Vael's order meant abundance. The beat is uncomfortable sympathy—the antagonist is a survivor too.

chapters.title: The Thirteenth Turn
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. On the equinox, with the valley fallen, Astrid reaches Wren at the standing stone where the original oath was sworn. The beat is desperate stillness before the storm—everything converges on one choice.

chapters.title: Speak, Little Bird
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren begins the waking-words but falters, and Astrid joins in—not perfectly, humanly, breaking the language's absolute power. The beat is transcendent defiance: imperfection as salvation.

chapters.title: Vael Wakes
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The god returns—but shaped by Wren's flawed, loving pronunciation: a presence that asks permission instead of demanding worship. Ilse shatters; Maren kneels willingly. The beat is awe tempered by uncertainty.

chapters.title: The Reckoning of Names
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The broken oath demands its price: Astrid's memories of everyone ever loved begin dissolving. The beat is quiet devastation—Astrid says goodbye to faces while still looking at them.

chapters.title: What Remains When Memory Fails
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren vows to become Astrid's memory, writing down every story Astrid tells before it fades. The beat is tender purpose—the child becomes the keeper of the keeper.

chapters.title: Spire and Choir
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The final confrontation with Ilse atop the ruined spire: she demands the old god back, and Astrid offers her instead a place in the new asking-world. The beat is hard-won mercy over vengeance.

chapters.title: The Valley Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Spring comes; the mist lifts permanently. Astrid, memoryless but not soulless, plants a garden while Wren reads aloud the stories of who Astrid was. The beat is gentle hope—identity outlives memory when someone carries it for you.
